description_ru: Комичная хроника сборки шкафа из магазина: бесконечные детали, загадочная инструкция и неожиданный финал.
text:
The box was delivered on a Thursday, and I remember thinking that it looked rather small for a wardrobe. This was my first error, and it was the sort of error that I would go on to repeat, with minor variations, for the next eleven hours. The box was not small. It was merely flat, and dense, in the way that a polite person is sometimes dense when you ask them for directions. It weighed as much as a modest horse, and it took two delivery men and a short, intense conversation about their backs to get it into the hall.

"It's a doddle," said one of them, as he left. "Just follow the instructions." I should have noticed the look that passed between them.

The instructions, which I discovered when I opened the box, consisted of a single large sheet showing a cheerful cartoon man with no mouth. His expression, though barely suggested, was one of mild bewilderment. He appeared in every step, and in each step he was doing something faintly impossible, such as holding a panel the size of a door in one hand while turning a screw with the other. At the top of the page was a small symbol that I took to mean "this will take two people", and a second one that I took to mean "or one very determined person". I counted myself as the second.

The first stage was to identify the components. These were arranged, with typical Scandinavian restraint, in several plastic bags labelled with letters, and they included: forty-eight screws of three different lengths, twelve small wooden pegs, eight metal brackets that looked like something from a medieval torture chamber, and a little silver object which, to this day, I have been unable to identify. The instructions never mentioned it. It was clearly the most important part of the whole wardrobe, and I have since decided that it is the cause of everything.

I began, with remarkable optimism, at nine in the morning. Step one involved attaching two sides to a bottom panel. This went well, as I had been warned by my father that the beginning of any project is a kind of cruel honeymoon, designed to make you invest in it. By ten I had a frame. By eleven I had a frame that was, I realised, upside down. And by noon I had discovered that the pre-drilled holes in the back panel, which was meant to slide neatly into place, were located precisely where the cartoon man's elbow had told me they would not be.

I will spare you the details of the next two hours, but I would like it recorded that I tried the following: reading the instructions in reverse, reading them with my head tilted, reading them aloud in a clear voice as though the cartoon man might respond, and, at one stage, praying. None of these methods was effective. At two o'clock I phoned my brother, who is good with his hands, and who listened to my description of the situation with the patient sigh of a man who has witnessed such scenes before. "Is the silver thing in the right place?" he asked. "What silver thing?" I replied, and he sighed again, rather more heavily.

My brother arrived at four with a toolbox the size of a suitcase and the serenity of a surgeon. He looked at the wardrobe for a while and then looked at me. "You've built it backwards," he said. "The doors are meant to be on the other side." I stared at the structure, which was by now more or less recognisable as furniture, and understood that three hours of work would have to be dismantled by hand, in the correct order, using the small screwdriver that had come with the kit and which had, throughout, been quietly bending.

We worked until nine in the evening, with breaks for tea and, in my case, a certain amount of muttering. The wardrobe grew slowly in the middle of the bedroom, and at some stage we stood back and admired it, as two men admire a ship before launching. It had two doors, a long rail for hanging clothes and a drawer at the bottom. It stood perfectly upright. There was only one problem: we had not used the silver object, nor, as it turned out, eleven of the screws.

"Probably spares," said my brother, with the offhand confidence of someone who does not live there. I put the extra screws in a jar, where they remain, and I have since read that this is a well-known feature of flat-pack furniture, and that every household in the country possesses a drawer or a jar of mysterious leftovers, a kind of national collection that one day may be recognised by a museum.

The wardrobe has now been in my bedroom for a month, and I am pleased to report that it has not fallen on anyone. The doors open with a small, plaintive creak. When I walk past it at night, it leans, very slightly, in the manner of a person who has just heard something interesting. My brother says that this is normal, and that I should stop looking at it. I have tried to follow this advice, but I cannot help feeling that the wardrobe and I have unfinished business.

Last weekend my sister, who is moving house, asked whether I would help her put together a bookcase from the same shop. I told her that I would be delighted. Then I went into the bedroom, opened the jar of leftover screws, and counted them again. There were twelve now. I have no idea where the extra one came from, and I have decided, for the sake of my own sanity, not to ask.

focus_sounds.tip_ru: Открытый звук между а и э: рот широко открыт, язык низко: flat, back.
Язык между зубами. В three и thing без голоса; в this и that с голосом.
Выдох после начальных p, t, k: pegs, time.
idENtify, mysTERious: ударение внутри слова, не на первом слоге.

questions.question: What was on the instruction sheet?
questions.answer: A cartoon man with no mouth who looked bewildered.

questions.question: What mistake did the writer make with the frame?
questions.answer: He built it upside down and backwards.

questions.question: Who came to help and when?
What was left over after the wardrobe was finished?
questions.answer: A silver object and eleven screws.
